lead: HTML5 semantic elements are named containers that say what a region of a page is for. A header holds the masthead, nav holds a menu, main holds the unique content, and footer holds the copyright line. Before HTML5, authors wrote div boxes with class names, so only a human could guess the structure. Semantic tags expose that structure to screen readers, search engines and browser reading modes. HTML5 also plays video and audio with native tags, so no plugin is needed, and embeds another page with iframe. The same tags appear on news sites, course portals and video lesson pages.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for nesting and attributes, and Chapter 2.2 for links and images.

blocks.text: A semantic element names the job of the content inside it. Use the element that matches the job, not a div with a class.

items: header: masthead, logo and site name; may repeat inside an article.
nav: a block of major links; not every group of links.
main: the one block of content unique to this page; appears once.
section: a thematic group with its own heading; a section without a heading is usually wrong.
article: a self-contained item that could be syndicated, such as one news story; it has its own heading.
aside: related links or side notes that are not the main flow.
footer: copyright, contact or closing notes.

blocks.text: Source order for a simple page is header, nav, main, aside, footer. The figure shows that order. CSS can move these boxes later; source order keeps reading order correct.

Article versus section: an article stands alone and makes sense outside the page; a section groups related content inside a page. A story is an article; 'Related coverage' inside that story is a section if it has a heading.

items: figure with figcaption: an image, diagram or code listing plus its caption.
details with summary: a disclosure box; summary is the always-visible label.
time: a date or time; the datetime attribute gives machine-readable form.
mark: text highlighted for reference.
progress: completion of a task, value between 0 and max.
meter: a measurement inside a known range, such as disk use.

blocks.text: Landmark regions read by assistive technology are header, nav, main, aside and footer. A section becomes a region only when it has an accessible name.
The video element plays a movie inside the page. The audio element plays sound only. Both take child source elements.

items: src: file path when using one file; with several sources, put src on source children.
controls: show browser play, pause and volume controls.
autoplay: start when the page loads; browsers block it unless muted is also present.
muted: start with sound off.
loop: restart at the end.
preload: hint, none, metadata or auto, for how much to fetch early.
poster: image shown before play; video only.

blocks.text: Use several source children when formats differ. The browser takes the first file it can play. The type attribute names the format, such as video/mp4 or video/webm. A 90-second clip in MP4 and WebM gives two source lines and one video element.

track adds captions or subtitles. kind='captions' gives sound descriptions and speech for deaf viewers; kind='subtitles' translates dialogue. srclang names the language, label is the menu name, and default picks the starting track. A caption file is WebVTT text.

Audio uses the same controls, autoplay, muted, loop and preload attributes, and source children. Poster, width and height belong to video. A browser that cannot play either format shows the fallback text between the tags.
An iframe embeds another HTML page inside a rectangular window. It is used for maps, video players and payment forms from another site.

items: src: URL of the embedded page.
title: short name read by screen readers; required in practice.
width and height: size in pixels; CSS can also set them.
sandbox: restricts the frame; an empty sandbox blocks scripts, forms and popups. Add tokens such as allow-scripts only when needed.

blocks.text: Old HTML used frameset with frame children to split the window into fixed panes. Frameset is obsolete; iframe replaces it for one embedded region. Old exam questions still expect that sentence. marquee is also obsolete; use CSS animation instead.
Two drawing tags complete the picture. canvas is a blank pixel grid drawn by JavaScript. Inline svg carries shapes as elements in the DOM. Both are alternatives to images for charts and icons.

figure.caption: Source order runs header, nav, main, aside, footer; the main region holds the article, and CSS may move aside visually without changing reading order.

spec.aria: Five semantic regions stacked in source order: header, nav, main, aside, footer.

examples.question: Mark up a news page made of five blocks: a masthead with the site name, a menu of four links, one story with a heading and two paragraphs, a sidebar of three related links, and a copyright line. Name the semantic element for each block, give the nesting order, and say which are landmark regions. Then add a 90-second video with controls, a poster image and a caption track.
steps: Block 1, masthead: use header with an h1 for the site name.
Block 2, menu: use nav with a ul of four li links. Link count = 4.
Block 3, story: use main containing one article. The article holds an h2 and two p elements.
Block 4, sidebar: use aside with three related links. Total links = 4 + 3 = 7.
Nesting order: body then header, nav, main with article, aside, footer as siblings. Landmarks: header, nav, main, aside, footer; article is not a landmark.

Video: video controls poster='metro.jpg' preload='metadata' width='640' height='360' with two source children, one MP4 and one WebM, and one track kind='captions' src='metro-en.vtt' srclang='en' label='English' default. The 90 seconds is the clip length, not an attribute.
examples.answer: The page has 5 top-level semantic blocks and 7 links, and the story carries a 90-second video with controls, a poster and 1 caption track.
examples.check:
top_blocks = 5
menu_links = 4
sidebar_links = 3
total_links = menu_links + sidebar_links
video_seconds = 90
caption_tracks = 1
print(top_blocks)
print(total_links)
print(video_seconds)
print(caption_tracks)

traps: Writing div class='header' where header belongs removes a landmark; use the named element.
Scattering section with no heading; a section needs a heading, or use div for styling only.
Treating article and section as synonyms; an article stands alone, a section groups inside a page.
Expecting autoplay to start with sound; modern browsers need muted too.
Forgetting that frameset is obsolete; old papers want iframe as the replacement.

quiz.q: Which element holds the page's unique content and appears once?
Why does a section need a heading?
quiz.a: The heading names the section and gives it a place in the outline; without one it is just an unnamed box.

quiz.q: A page has header, nav with 3 links, main with one article, aside with 2 links, and footer. Give the total links and the landmark regions.
quiz.a: 3 + 2 = 5 links. Landmarks: header, nav, main, aside, footer; article is not a landmark.

quiz.q: Write the opening video tag for a clip with controls, a poster, and two sources (MP4 and WebM).
quiz.a: video controls poster='pic.jpg' width='640' height='360' with source src='clip.mp4' type='video/mp4' and source src='clip.webm' type='video/webm' inside.

quiz.q: A story has two comment blocks, each with a heading. Should the story be an article and the comments sections, or all sections?
quiz.a: The story is an article because it stands alone. Each comment block is a section inside it because it groups part of that story and has a heading.

quiz.q: What does an empty sandbox attribute on an iframe block?
quiz.a: It blocks scripts, forms, popups and top-level navigation; the embedded page can still display its static content.

beyond: Not for the exam. Browser makers now treat HTML as a living standard, so semantic elements gain details without version numbers. Web Components let authors define new custom elements with shadow DOM, which changes how page structure is exposed. Video on the web also involves DRM, adaptive streaming and WebVTT caption styling. Iframes matter for security because sandbox and allow attributes limit embedded third-party code. Search next for the HTML Living Standard sections on semantic elements, WebVTT and iframe sandbox.
